title: India's Aviation Boom Hits Turbulence as Safety Lapses and Losses Mount
excerpt: A parliamentary panel found 100 safety lapses at Air India and the DGCA flagged dozens more across carriers, as airlines face nearly $4 billion in combined losses.
body:
• India's aviation sector — celebrated as one of the country's biggest success stories — is straining under safety lapses, mounting losses and infrastructure that has not kept pace with growth.
  • A parliamentary panel found around 100 safety lapses at Air India, including seven needing "urgent corrective action" and pilot training gaps on Boeing 787 and 777 fleets.
  • The DGCA's annual audit reported 93 lapses at Air India, 23 at IndiGo and 14 at SpiceJet, including maintenance work orders not followed.
  • ICRA estimates Indian airlines will lose nearly $4 billion this fiscal year; Air India's losses more than doubled to $2.3 billion last fiscal.

Indian airlines carried about 167 million passengers last year — more than double the figure a decade earlier. More than 70 airports have been added in ten years, and carriers have some 1,500 aircraft on order. But behind the boom, a string of safety lapses, financial strain and operational chaos is raising hard questions about whether the sector's foundations can support its ambitions.

An audit of Air India identified around 100 safety lapses, including seven violations requiring "urgent corrective action" and "recurrent training gaps" for Boeing 787 and 777 pilots, according to a parliamentary panel report cited by AFP.

What the audits found

The Directorate General of Civil Aviation's annual sectoral safety audit in July exposed repeated defects, ineffective monitoring and maintenance issues across carriers: 93 lapses at Air India, 23 at IndiGo and 14 at SpiceJet. Auditors found a maintenance work order had not been followed, and in one case a domestic flight was held up because of worn tyres.

Other episodes bordered on the farcical while exposing serious shortcomings: a forgotten Air India aircraft was rediscovered after sitting parked at a major airport for over a decade, and another was found flying without necessary documentation, according to local media reports.

"At present, everyone is paying lip service to safety. By paying lip service, you do not create a safety culture."

— Shakti Lumba, former airline operations chief

Former Air India executive director Jitender Bhargava said a reported drug case involving crew raised questions about management oversight, arguing the pilot community would know if a colleague was impaired.

Money troubles compound safety troubles

The safety concerns arrive as airlines grapple with severe financial pressure. Indian carriers have faced the closure of Pakistani airspace since tensions escalated last year, forcing longer and costlier routings. Rising jet fuel prices linked to the Middle East conflict have added to the strain.

Ratings agency ICRA estimates Indian airlines will lose nearly $4 billion this fiscal year. Air India's losses more than doubled to $2.3 billion in the last fiscal year, while IndiGo has reported losses for two consecutive quarters. IndiGo last month shut down its wide-body operations, and Air India is reportedly considering delaying deliveries of as many as 500 aircraft.

A system stretched thin

"The problem has not been a lack of growth," said Harsh Vardhan, chairman of Starair Consulting. "It is that every other part of the ecosystem has not been able to keep up with this growth and manage it well."

The strain has shown up operationally: IndiGo cancelled large numbers of flights after failing to prepare for new pilot fatigue regulations, despite having a full year to plan. The government's ambition — a fleet growing from 400 aircraft in 2014 to over 2,300 by 2040, and up to 400 airports — depends on regulatory bandwidth and infrastructure catching up with demand.

What it means for travellers

For the diaspora, which flies these routes more than almost anyone, the takeaway is vigilance rather than alarm: India's skies remain statistically safe, but the audit trail suggests a system running hot. Rapid demand and fleet growth without matching regulatory and infrastructure build-out produces systemic fragility, analysts warn — and the recent crises should be treated as a turning point, not a blip.
